description:
Who We Are: A multidisciplinary team ready for Space Apps.
Skills: Kayra & Arda (AI, software, multimedia), Emre & Ömer (Academic research), Talha (Avionics, sensors, hardware).
Why Us: We turn raw data into working tech with clear pitches.
Looking For: UI/UX Designers, Data Scientists, and Presenters.
summary:
SPARK is a health monitor that astronauts use themselves when Earth is delayed or out of reach. Its Main screen shows each crew member’s blood pressure, HRV, SpO₂, temperature and mental state, plus cabin CO₂, inspired O₂, pressure and radiation. Five features carry the project:

Early Warning forecasts each health value from its last two weeks, using daily averages and a Theil–Sen trend. It tells the astronaut when a value would reach a limit, with matching advice.
Mission readiness panel combines sleep, HRV, cognitive test and cabin CO₂ into a 0–100 score for the next critical task, with a red gate for single failures.
Cabin radiation panel compares career, 30-day organ and solar-event doses against NASA limits. It also calculates radiation information for the existing planned route, such as the route ratio, each astronaut’s own dose and an EVA decision for the planned EVA day.
EVA screen tracks return time, consumables and suit values. It adds an Orthostatic Risk Index (ORI) that lowered false alarms on real PhysioNet data from 9 of 10 recordings to 1 of 10.
Acute question sequence: the Emergency button leads through short questions to checklist instructions and an automatic SBAR package.
details:
SPARK is a decision-support prototype for crew health on deep-space missions. It is not a diagnostic device. It shows who is affected, how much time they have, and what to do, even when the link to Earth is delayed or lost.

How it works: The app has eight views: Main, Personal, Tasks & Calendar, Periodic, Physical, Cabin, EVA and Emergency. Alerts use three colour-coded levels. Critical alerts notify the astronaut, the health screen and Earth, and they queue while the link is down. Our five main features are:

  • Early Warning forecasts each health value from its last two weeks and says when it would reach a limit. It gives the astronaut simple instructions to prevent likely health problems.
  • Mission readiness panel turns sleep, HRV, cognitive test and cabin CO₂ into a go/no-go score.
  • Cabin radiation panel compares career, 30-day organ and solar-event doses against NASA limits. It also calculates radiation information for the existing planned route, such as the route ratio, each astronaut’s own dose and an EVA decision for the planned EVA day.
  • EVA panel shows nine suit metrics, including an Orthostatic Risk Index, on a glove-friendly keyboard layout.
  • Emergency sequence is a decision tree of 115 questions leading to 64 instruction cards.

Benefits and impact: Crews on the Moon or Mars cannot count on real-time ground support. SPARK gives them decision support that works on its own and shows where each limit comes from. All alert limits and instructions are drafts awaiting flight-surgeon approval.

Tools: TypeScript, Vite, three.js for the 3D body model, Electron for the desktop app, Python and Node.js scripts for data, browser localStorage (no server), and unit tests. The data comes from NASA OSDR RadLab and Inspiration4, DONKI, NOAA GOES, PhysioNet and BodyParts3D. All crew data is fictional and labelled on screen as sample data.

Creative factors:

Crew Oxygen Chart. When oxygen falls, the first question is whether the problem is one person or life support. This chart answers that at a glance. It stacks three layers on one time axis:

  • every astronaut’s SpO₂, with the selected person drawn thicker
  • cabin oxygen as inspired pressure (PIO₂), because the same percentage means less oxygen at lower pressure
  • cabin CO₂ as a 1-hour average

If one line drops, check that person and their sensor. If several lines drop together, check the cabin air first. Caution and critical bands come from NASA-STD-3001, and the chart can show 1 h, 6 h or 24 h.

Mission Readiness Panel. People rarely notice their own fatigue, so this panel uses measurements instead of feelings. It answers one question: is this person ready for the next critical task, such as an EVA, robotic arm work or docking?

  • Score: a 0–100 weighted mean of sleep (40 %), HRV (25 %), cognitive test (25 %) and cabin CO₂ (10 %).
  • Status: 70 and above is Ready, 50–69 is Caution, below 50 is Not ready.
  • Red gate: a single red factor, such as less than 5 h of sleep before an EVA, blocks the card whatever the total.
  • Transparency: the panel shows how many points each factor takes off, with the biggest loss in bold, so the crew sees why, not just what.

A dedicated EVA screen. Health monitoring should not stop at the hatch, so we built a second monitor for spacewalks.

  • Return by: the top card shows how long the astronaut can stay out, set by the scarcest resource (O₂, battery), with the margin after the walk back.
  • Six vital tiles: O₂, suit pressure, inspired CO₂, workload, heat and orthostatic risk. Each tile shows its status by colour, with its thresholds in the corner.
  • Glove-friendly controls: the whole screen runs on five physical keys, with no mouse or touch. Safety actions such as starting the return or raising an emergency need a 3-second hold, so they cannot be pressed by accident.
  • Checklist bar and partner line: these keep the task and the buddy’s status in view.

ORI (Orthostatic Risk Index). ORI is a 0–100 score for how likely the astronaut is to become dizzy or faint when posture or gravity changes. This is a real risk after weightlessness, for example when first standing or walking on Mars.

  • Inputs: ORI combines six physiological loads into one weighted score: autonomic reserve (HRV against the person’s own baseline), heart-rate deviation, vasodilation (core–skin temperature gradient), heat storage, volume deficit and blood-pressure trend.
  • Levels: above 60 is Caution, above 80 is Critical. The Health Hexagon shows which load is pushing the score up.
  • Version 1.1 changes: in version 1.0, healthy volunteers in real PhysioNet tilt-test data (PRCP) triggered false alarms in 9 of 10 recordings. Version 1.1 brought that down to 1 of 10. It does this with a personal blood-pressure limit instead of one value for everyone, a posture gate that stops orthostatic alarms while sitting or lying, and an EVA mode that removes the effect of physical effort from heart rate, so hard work is not mistaken for circulatory stress.

Cabin Radiation Panel: three mission situations. Radiation risk depends on where the spacecraft is, so the panel follows the existing route and has one tab per situation:

  1. Low Earth orbit (ISS type): it shows the current radiation index and the time to the next South Atlantic Anomaly pass. It warns “Do not start an EVA” for each pass and proposes safe EVA windows of at least 6.5 h, drawn on a world map with the orbit track.
  2. Lunar transit (Artemis I type): it marks the Van Allen belt crossings. Inside the inner belt it shows a Critical state: no EVA, crew outside return to the airlock, everyone goes to the most shielded place. A replay with a slider shows the position between Earth and Moon and the route risk.
  3. Mars transit (our mission): in galactic cosmic rays there is no radiation zone, so only a solar particle event (live NOAA GOES strip) or a person’s own dose can stop an EVA. A table gives each astronaut’s EVA decision for the planned EVA day.

All three tabs judge each astronaut by their worst dose ratio against NASA limits, never an average.

Emergency button and acute question sequence. On a deep-space mission the link to Earth can be delayed or lost exactly when something goes wrong. The Emergency button on the Main screen asks one question: is it a cabin or environment problem, or a health problem?

  • Question tree: for a health problem, a short sequence of plain-language questions (115 in the full tree) leads to one of 64 instruction cards. These are 15 Emergency, 17 Priority and 32 Monitor.
  • Instruction cards: each card has “Do now” steps with Done buttons, “While waiting for communication” monitoring, and “If it gets worse” escalation, for example to CPR.
  • Automatic records: the panel reads sensor values itself and prepares an SBAR package for Earth automatically.
  • Who can use it: any crew member, not only a doctor, can act with confidence when it matters most.

How we meet the challenge’s considerations

  • Different environments: the system works inside the spacecraft and on a planetary surface (EVA screen, Mars surface). The radiation panel covers low Earth orbit, lunar transit and Mars transit.
  • Prompting measurements and actions: the Periodic screen lists recurring health tasks, adds them to each astronaut’s calendar automatically, and marks them Due and then Overdue after 7 days. The daily check-in asks for sleep, symptoms and mood morning and evening.
  • Gamification: a “chain-breaking” streak counts consecutive check-in days and appears on the Tasks & Calendar screen. Crew and family birthdays are on the calendar to support morale.
  • Dynamic charts: the oxygen, readiness, radiation, cabin, lab and reaction-time charts all show trends over selectable ranges (1 h to the whole mission). Early Warning projects each value forward and says when it would reach a limit.
  • Colour coding: green, yellow and red are used throughout. Every value shows its status at a glance, and a day/night colour mode helps keep circadian rhythm.
  • Simple instructions and explanations: every value shows its limit and source. The 3D body model shows where a problem is and lists the values for that region with their limits. Each periodic task explains how to do it. The emergency cards give step-by-step instructions in plain language, with no medical training assumed.
